metaDescription: Odoo IoT box setup for scales, receipt and label printers, scanners and card terminals. Enterprise only. What is supported, what breaks, and country notes.
intro: Odoo IoT is the bridge between Odoo and physical hardware on a counter or a shop floor. A small Linux box sits on the same local network as the tills or work centres, talks to devices over USB, Bluetooth or the network, and presents them to Odoo as named devices you assign to a point of sale, a work centre or a quality control point. The app is Enterprise only.

Most of the effort goes on hardware decisions, not configuration screens. Odoo ships drivers for a specific set of printers, scales and terminals, and a device outside that set needs a handler written for it or does not work. Choosing hardware before the network, the acquirer contract and the local fiscal rules are settled is how these projects lose a month.

It helps to treat the box as a translator rather than a controller. Odoo asks for a print or a reading, the box speaks the device's language and hands the answer back. Nothing of yours is stored there, nothing of yours runs on a schedule there. Once that is agreed, most scoping arguments settle themselves: anything needing buffered history, a control loop or a machine protocol belongs in a PLC or a separate collector, and the box carries only the result into a transaction.
whoFor: Retailers and restaurants needing the printer, drawer, customer display and card terminal to act as one till.
Butchers, delis and packing halls that price by weight and want the scale reading in the order line.
Manufacturers whose work order steps need a measurement, a photo, a printed label or a footswitch.
Warehouses printing shipping and product labels at the packing bench instead of from a driver installed on one desktop.
Not for plant telemetry or condition monitoring. The box moves a single event or reading into a transaction, it does not sample a signal all day.
Not for Community, where the app is absent and only direct network printing from Point of Sale is available.

capabilities.title: Point of sale hardware behaving as one till
capabilities.body: Assign a receipt printer, cash drawer, barcode scanner, electronic scale and customer display to a point of sale configuration and the session drives all of them. The drawer opens on the kick signal from the printer rather than through its own cable, which is why a drawer that will not open is usually a printer problem. Products flagged as sold by weight open the scale screen at the till, so the cashier confirms a live reading instead of typing a number.

capabilities.title: Card terminals, and which of them need the box
capabilities.body: Terminal support routes differently by acquirer, and that decides whether you buy a box at all. Ingenico and Worldline terminals reach Odoo through the IoT box on the local network. Adyen and Stripe connect over the internet with no box involved. Recent versions also ship Razorpay and Paytm terminal support for the Indian market, again without a box. In every integrated case Odoo pushes the amount and reads the result back, so the figure on the terminal cannot drift from the figure on the order.

capabilities.title: Measurement in production and quality
capabilities.body: A quality control point of the measure type can read from a connected gauge instead of a keyboard, which takes the typed number out of the audit trail and out of the argument later. Work order steps do the same, and can print a label or capture a photograph from a USB camera at the step that requires it. Work centres carry IoT triggers, so a footswitch or a barcode scan advances the operator without gloved hands on a tablet.

capabilities.title: Label and report printing without a driver on every PC
capabilities.body: A printer attached to the box becomes a destination Odoo sends to directly, and a report can be pointed at a named IoT printer. Zebra units are addressed with ZPL and receipt printers with ESC/POS. A delivery slip and a shipping label then leave from different machines without an operator picking a printer from a dialog. That removes the pattern where a label is downloaded as a PDF and collected from a printer in the wrong room.

capabilities.title: Scanners, and when they need the box at all
capabilities.body: Most USB and Bluetooth scanners present as a keyboard, type the barcode into whatever field has focus and need no box. The Barcode app and the point of sale both read them that way. Configure the scanner to send a carriage return as a suffix, or consecutive scans run together into one string. The box earns its place when the scanner has to sit away from the machine running the browser, or when a scan is a work centre trigger rather than text in a field.

capabilities.title: Running the box, or running without one
capabilities.body: The box is a Raspberry Pi image tied to one Odoo major version, so it is upgraded when the database is, not whenever it suits. Where a Pi is impractical, the Windows virtual IoT service gives the same endpoint on a machine already sitting at the counter. For hardware Odoo does not cover, a Python handler shipped inside a custom module is pulled down by the box on connection, so the driver travels with the code rather than living on an SD card that someone reflashed.

setup.title: Network first, hardware second
setup.body: The box and the browser running Odoo have to reach each other on the same local network. Give the box a reserved DHCP address, keep it off any guest VLAN and off client isolation, and run cable rather than WiFi to a till that matters. Shop floor WiFi with roaming access points is the reason a device works in a quiet test and disappears at a trading peak.

setup.title: The certificate step people skip
setup.body: Odoo is served over HTTPS, and a browser will not call a box on plain HTTP from an HTTPS page. The box requests a certificate for its own odoo-iot.com subdomain, and that request only succeeds against a database with a valid Enterprise subscription. On a trial or unlinked test database the box stays on HTTP, the browser blocks the call without an obvious error, and no device ever responds. Pair against the real subscription first, then clone for testing.

setup.title: Confirm the acquirer supports an integrated terminal
setup.body: A terminal is only integrable if the bank loaded the right application onto it. The same model ships in integrated or standalone mode and only the acquirer can change that. Get the model, the protocol and the merchant account confirmed in writing before anything is ordered. Where no integration exists the terminal stays standalone and the cashier records the tender by hand, which is a workable answer as long as it is priced and trained for rather than discovered in week eleven.

setup.title: List what prints where, then name every device
setup.body: Write down each document that has to come out of a machine: receipt, kitchen ticket, product label, shipping label, invoice. Each carries a paper size, a printer language and a physical location. One station usually needs an ESC/POS receipt printer and a separate label printer rather than one device attempting both. Then name the devices to match the location, because point of sale configurations and reports reference those names, and a replacement box with different names means repointing every one of them.

setup.title: Prove the receipt on the real paper
setup.body: An ESC/POS receipt is not a shrunken PDF. It renders in the printer's own character set at a fixed width, so 58mm and 80mm are two different layouts, and logos, Arabic text and QR codes each behave differently again. Print the real receipt, on the real roll, from the real printer model before the layout is signed off. Leaving this until after the fiscal fields are added is what turns a formatting detail into a go-live delay.

pitfalls.title: One box, one point of failure
pitfalls.body: A single box serving four tills means four tills stop when it stops. SD cards in a Pi wear out and unstable mains will finish one off. Keep a spare flashed card and a written pairing procedure at each site. Restoring a box is a twenty minute job for somebody who has done it before and a lost trading day for somebody reading the manual for the first time.

pitfalls.title: A box pairs to one database
pitfalls.body: The box connects to a single Odoo database. Point a test database at the same box while training is running and the two compete for the devices, with prints landing in the wrong session and pairings dropping. Either give the test environment its own box, or accept that hardware testing happens on production hardware in a booked window. Deciding that in advance is cheaper than discovering it during user training.

pitfalls.title: Scales that cannot be read, or cannot legally be used
pitfalls.body: Two separate problems get merged into one line on a plan. The first is protocol: Odoo reads a short list of scale protocols, and a counter scale with a proprietary serial output needs a handler written against it. The second is legal. Selling by weight requires a trade approved instrument in most markets, and an approved scale is a different purchase at a different price from a parcel scale. Check both before ordering, not after.

pitfalls.title: The browser session is part of the hardware
pitfalls.body: Devices are reached from the browser, so an operator who closes the tab, opens a second session or lets a laptop sleep loses the printer. Kiosk mode, a machine set never to suspend and a station login that stays open are configuration items rather than refinements. Tablets that drop WiFi when the screen goes off produce faults that look random to the user and are entirely predictable once the cause is known.

pitfalls.title: Version drift between box and database
pitfalls.body: The box image is built for one Odoo major version. Upgrade the database, leave the boxes on last year's image, and devices list but stop responding without a clear error. Put a reflash of every box into the upgrade weekend, count the sites honestly including the one in the back office nobody logged, and confirm each device model still has a driver in the target version before a date is promised to anyone.

pitfalls.title: Nobody owns the box after go-live
pitfalls.body: The box sits on the customer's local network, behind their firewall, plugged into their counter. That places it outside what a hosting provider supports, whether the database runs on Odoo Online, Odoo.sh or your own server. Name the person who reflashes a card, who holds the spare, and who is called when a printer stops at 08:00 on a Saturday. Hardware support scope is worth one paragraph in the contract and saves a long argument later.

worksWith: Point of Sale, for printers, drawers, scales, scanners, customer displays and terminals
Point of Sale Restaurant, where order printers send each line to the station that prepares it
Manufacturing work orders, for measurements, labels, photographs and footswitch triggers
Quality, where a measure type control point reads from a gauge rather than a keyboard
Inventory and Barcode, for scan driven picking and labels printed at the packing bench
Fiscal localisation modules, which decide what a compliant receipt has to carry
Acquirer terminals from Ingenico, Worldline, Adyen and Stripe, each reaching Odoo by a different route

regional.note: ZATCA Phase 2 decides what a till may print. Simplified B2C invoices carry a QR code and are reported to Fatoora within twenty four hours, so the layout has to render Arabic and English together on 80mm paper and still fit the QR. The box only prints. Reporting runs from the point of sale localisation module, which makes an offline till a compliance question rather than only an operational one.

There is no fiscal device rule at the counter, so hardware here is an operations decision rather than a compliance one. The constraint is the acquirer. Terminals supplied by Network International and Magnati are not in Odoo's supported list, so most retail runs the terminal standalone and the cashier selects the payment method by hand, unless a driver is written for the exact model the bank issues.

The Egyptian Tax Authority runs two schemes: e-invoicing for B2B documents and a separate e-receipt system for retail sales. Odoo's official Egyptian modules address invoices rather than e-receipts, so submitting point of sale receipts means a third party apps store module or a build against the ETA specification. Budget the compliance link and the hardware as two work packages with two owners.

FBR digital invoicing sits between the till and the printed receipt. Integrated Tier-1 retailers report each sale in real time, and the receipt shows the fiscal invoice number and QR that FBR returns, so a sale is not finished until the call comes back. Decide in advance what the cashier does when it does not. Integration runs through PRAL or a licensed integrator and is a separate track from the hardware.

Weighing is where a box earns its keep. Any instrument used to price a sale must be verified and stamped under the Legal Metrology Act, with re-verification on a cycle, and a parcel scale bought online will not qualify. GST reporting and e-invoicing are handled in accounting rather than at the counter, so the hardware track and the compliance track can run in parallel without either waiting on the other.

Retail is regulated at the device. Consumer sales are recorded on a certified new generation payment recording device, the YN OKC, bought from a licensed vendor, which signs and stores the receipt using its own fiscal certificate. Odoo has no driver for these devices, so an IoT receipt printer does not satisfy the rule on its own. Scope this as an integration to the approved device, with the vendor in the room from the first workshop.

Every electronic till needs a certified technical security element under the Kassensicherungsverordnung, along with a DSFinV-K export and GoBD traceability. Odoo signs point of sale orders through a certified cloud TSE provider and produces the DSFinV-K file, and that provider is a paid subscription separate from the Odoo licence. Because a receipt must be offered for every sale, a working printer at each till is a legal requirement rather than a convenience.

The anti fraud rule under CGI article 286 I-3 bis requires a certified and unalterable cash system, and Odoo ships l10n_fr_pos_cert for it. Once an order is posted it is hashed into a chain and locked, so a wrongly rung sale is corrected with a refund and never by editing the record. Reprints stay traceable, which means a duplicate receipt comes off the till through the proper action rather than from a saved PDF.

faqs.q: Do I need an IoT box just to print a receipt?
faqs.a: Not always. Point of Sale can print straight to a network Epson TM printer using the Epson ePOS support, with no box on the network. The box becomes necessary for a drawer driven from the printer, for scales, for integrated Ingenico or Worldline terminals, and for dependable label printing at a bench that has no PC beside it.

faqs.q: Is Odoo IoT available in Community?
faqs.a: No. The IoT app is part of Odoo Enterprise, as are the modules that connect it to Point of Sale, Manufacturing and Quality. Community can still use keyboard emulating scanners and network printing from Point of Sale. Assigned devices, live scale readings, gauge input on quality checks and integrated card terminals are Enterprise only, and no community module reproduces them.

faqs.q: Can I keep the scale I already own?
faqs.a: Only if Odoo has a driver for the protocol it speaks, and that list is short. Anything outside it needs a handler written against the instrument's serial output, which is contained work once the manufacturer supplies the protocol document. Ask for that document before assuming the scale can be reused, because some manufacturers will not release it and that answer changes the hardware budget.

faqs.q: Do we need a box for barcode scanning?
faqs.a: Usually not. A scanner in keyboard emulation mode types into the focused field and works in the Barcode app and at the till with no box. Set the suffix to a carriage return during commissioning. A box is worth it when the scanner sits away from the machine running the browser, or when the scan has to fire a work centre trigger rather than fill a field.

faqs.q: Can one box serve our test database and the live one?
faqs.a: No. A box pairs to a single database. Running training on a copy while production uses the same box causes prints to land in the wrong session and pairings to drop. Buy a second box for the test environment, or agree that hardware testing happens against production in a booked window with the tills closed.

faqs.q: Can we run this on Windows instead of a Raspberry Pi?
faqs.a: Yes. The Windows virtual IoT service installs on a machine already at the counter and exposes the same endpoint, which suits a back office that has a PC and no room for another appliance. The trade is that Windows updates, sleep settings and antivirus become part of your till. A Pi does one job and is replaced from a spare card in minutes.

faqs.q: How many devices can one box handle?
faqs.a: There is no published limit, and the practical constraint is USB power and network stability rather than software. Retail usually runs one box per till so a failure stays local to one lane. In a warehouse, one box serving several printers is normal, because a print job can wait a few seconds in a queue and a customer at a till cannot.

faqs.q: What happens at the till if the box goes offline?
faqs.a: The session keeps taking orders, because Point of Sale runs in the browser and holds orders locally. What stops is everything that needs hardware: printing, the drawer, the scale and any terminal routed through the box. Cash sales become the immediate problem, since the drawer is driven by the printer. A spare flashed SD card on site matters more than a spare printer.

faqs.q: Can the box read data from a production machine?
faqs.a: Only through something that presents as a serial, USB or network device with a driver behind it. There is no Modbus or OPC UA support out of the box, no historian and no alarming. For genuine machine data, collect it in a system built for that, then feed a summarised figure or a pass and fail result into Odoo where it attaches to a work order.
